policies.summary: No local zoning ordinance or bylaw may prohibit or unreasonably regulate solar energy systems except where necessary to protect public health, safety or welfare.

For large clean energy facilities, the siting board consolidated permit stands in for all municipal, regional and state permits, and is deemed granted if the board misses its deadline; for small facilities, local governments must apply uniform state standards and a missed 12-month deadline produces a constructive approval.
policies.statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T(i); ch. 25A, section 21(b), (d) to (g)

policies.summary: The Energy Facilities Siting Board issues a single consolidated permit for solar and wind facilities of 25 MW or more (solar measured in DC) and storage of 100 MWh or more; smaller clean energy facilities are permitted by the city or town under uniform state standards, with a 12-month deadline and de novo review by the siting division director.
policies.statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T; ch. 25A, section 21 (as added or amended by St. 2024, c. 239)

restrictions.description: Town wanted time to study where BESS can be built and what rules should govern them -- public safety, fire protection, drinking water, farm/forest impacts, and rural character -- amid a wave of BESS/solar development proposals in neighboring Hilltowns (Worthington, Plainfield) ahead of new state fast-track solar-permitting rules effective 2026-10-01. Approaching its scheduled end as of 2026-09-23. The June 24, 2026 temporary moratorium on BESS construction runs through 2026-09-30; that same evening the town has scheduled a further Special Town Meeting to vote on a permanent BESS zoning bylaw (finalized by the Planning Board on 2026-09-15), which if adopted would supersede the moratorium and would still require Attorney General approval. As of the July 7, 2026 Gazette roundup, the June 24 moratorium itself 'now awaits approval from the attorney general's office'; no confirmation that the AG approved or disapproved the temporary moratorium was located in this pass. Legal basis: Chesterfield Special Town Meeting warrant article adopting a temporary moratorium on construction of battery energy storage systems (BESS); specific article/bylaw number not located in sources reviewed.

Data centers undefined in Gill zoning bylaws; unique energy and noise impacts; related BESS state-regulatory uncertainty. Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted unanimously as Article 7 at the May 4, 2026 Annual Town Meeting (Part 1), establishing a one-year moratorium on Building-Integrated Energy Storage Systems (BESS) of 50 kWh or more and on Data Centers, running through 2027-05-03 or earlier supersession by new zoning. Town Counsel Donna MacNicol told voters before the vote that the BESS portion was unlikely to survive Attorney General review because standalone BESS is treated as a protected/solar-adjacent use under G.L. c. 48, Section 3, and recommended splitting the article into two motions; voters instead approved the combined article as written (several Massachusetts towns, including Blandford, Worthington, and Wendell, had similar BESS moratoria disapproved by the AGO's Municipal Law Unit in 2026). No Attorney General Municipal Law Unit decision specific to this Gill bylaw was located as of 2026-09-23. The Gill Planning Board's Sept. 17, 2026 meeting agenda lists 'Review Data Centers for bylaw updates,' consistent with continuing work toward permanent regulations during the moratorium period. Legal basis: Gill Zoning Bylaws Section 18, Building-Integrated Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Data Centers, adopted as Article 7 of the May 4, 2026 Annual Town Meeting warrant (Part 1).

Need to study BESS and data centers and develop zoning controls consistent with state siting and permitting requirements. Still not enacted as of 2026-09-23. The proposed Section 6.11 BESS/Data Center moratorium, noticed for a March 11, 2026 Planning Board public hearing, was withdrawn before the final May 9, 2026 Annual Town Meeting warrant was signed: the town's own signed warrant (FINAL_SIGNED_2026_ATM-ATE_WARRANT) lists only 22 articles, none addressing BESS or data centers, and Greenfield Recorder confirms voters took up 'nearly all 22 warrant articles,' with only the meeting-posting bylaw (Article 20) defeated. At its April 1, 2026 meeting, the Planning Board discussed whether to 'work on a moratorium, or go straight to creating the bylaws' via Special Town Meeting instead. By its May 6, 2026 meeting (three days before Annual Town Meeting), the Board was discussing scheduling a further public hearing on 'a moratorium for large scale battery storage systems' (data centers no longer named in that agenda item). No subsequent public-hearing notice, warrant article, or Town Meeting vote on a BESS or data-center moratorium was located through 2026-09-23; the town's website listed no Special Town Meeting scheduled as of the research date. Legal basis: Proposed Zoning Bylaw Section 6.11, submitted by Planning Board and recommended by Select Board.

Community and Council concern over AI data centers' potential environmental and buffer-zone impacts, and over battery storage facility fire risk; no data center or large-scale battery storage project is currently proposed in Leominster. Part of a regional wave of central Massachusetts data-center/BESS moratoria (Fitchburg, Athol). Pending as of 2026-09-23. The City Council held a public hearing on the combined data-center/BESS moratorium petitions on 2026-09-14; the Planning Board had not yet delivered its recommendation, and the Council unanimously granted more time, scheduling a further hearing/vote for 2026-09-28 (five days after this research pass). Mayor Mazzarella has not indicated support and has publicly cautioned against rushing the petitions. [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.65 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: City Council petitions for a one-year-equivalent moratorium (through July 31, 2027) on data centers and battery energy storage facilities; would also require Mayor Dean Mazzarella's approval before taking effect. Petition instrument number not confirmed in sources reviewed.

State model BESS ordinance and Oct. 1, 2026 state deadline for local consolidated-permit ordinances; no local BESS regulations existed. Active as of 2026-09-23; set to expire Sept. 30, 2026 (about one week after this research date) unless extended or superseded by the separate permanent BESS zoning amendment still in committee. Legal basis: Municipal Code Section 5-31, Interim Restriction for Battery Energy Storage Systems.

The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones.

In 2019, residents of the Town of Charlton voted at a town meeting to cap the number of large-scale solar installations in the town at the number currently approved (30 total), thus prohibiting new solar projects.

In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws.
Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions.

projects.description: In 2017, Avangrid began the development of two offshore wind farms south of Martha’s Vineyard – Commonwealth Wind (1,200-MW) and Park City Wind (800-MW).

In December 2024, Braintree’s fire chief declined to sign off on Convergent Energy’s 5-MW Battery Energy Storage System proposal, which would have been located 200 feet from a church and 159 feet from the nearest house.
Two turbines known as Falmouth Wind 1 and 2, which were installed in 2010 and 2013, faced opposition from neighbors based in part on concerns about noise and health impacts.

In 2016, the Town of Bourne filed suit against Future Generation Wind, claiming that the company was failing to consider the impacts in Bourne of a 4-turbine, 6-MW wind farm it was constructing in the neighboring town of Plymouth.
A group called Waltham Neighbors for Safe Solar is circulating a petition for restrictions on a planned 9-acre, 1-MW solar plant on the Lexington/Waltham border.

In July 2024, residents of Centerville, a village in the Town of Barnstable, filed a civil suit against the Barnstable Town Council seeking injunctive relief to stop the construction of transmission lines for Avangrid’s New England Wind 1 offshore wind project.
In September 2021, the Northfield Planning Board approved a proposal by BlueWave Solar for a solar energy project that would cover 76 acres on three noncontiguous tracts.

In August 2016, opponents of a proposed 6.2-MW solar farm filed a lawsuit in federal court alleging that the 30-acre site contained Native American burial grounds and that it was a ceremonial landscape.

projects.description: SouthCoast Wind is a proposed 2,400-MW offshore project that would be located 30 miles south of Martha’s Vineyard and 20 miles south of Nantucket.
In 2017, Avangrid Renewables proposed a 62-turbine, 800-MW offshore wind project located more than 15 miles of Martha’s Vineyard.
A local group called East Street Neighborhood Association formed in opposition to a proposed 1.8-MW solar project in West Bridgewater.
In September 2017, residents in the town of Savoy voted against an amendment that would have allowed Minuteman Wind LLC to extend the height of their turbines from 425 to 453 feet.
In 2019, PureSky Energy proposed the Cape Cod Solar project on approximately 83 acres (out of over 200 acres) of a former country club golf course in the Town of Falmouth.
In 2025, Lodestar Energy proposed the 3.5-MW Van Deusenville Solar Project to be located on a 12-acre parcel of land zoned as a residential district in the Town of Great Barrington.
In 2021, Sunpin Energy proposed the 4.3-MW Petersham Solar project to be located on approximately 14 acres in Petersham, Worcester County.
